coins.valuationNotes: The 1990 Roosevelt Dime is a common circulation coin with high mintage from both the Philadelphia and Denver mints. In standard circulated condition, it typically carries no numismatic premium and is worth only its face value. While a rare 'No S' proof variety exists for this year (lacking the San Francisco mint mark), it was only released in proof sets and is not found in general circulation. Standard circulated 1990 dimes are valued at $0.10.

The 1936 Lincoln Wheat Cent is a common date with a mintage of over 311 million. In standard circulated condition (Good to About Uncirculated), retail values range from $0.15 to $2.00. The most prominent variety for this year is the Doubled Die Obverse (DDO), specifically the FS-101, which exhibits strong doubling on the date and the word 'LIBERTY'. If the coin is confirmed as the FS-101 DDO variety, its value in circulated condition can range from $100 to over $400 depending on the specific grade.

The 2007 USA Dollar coins include the Sacagawea design and the first four releases of the Presidential $1 Coin Program: George Washington, John Adams, Thomas Jefferson, and James Madison. In standard circulated condition, these coins are generally worth only their face value. However, 2007 is well-known for the 'Missing Edge Lettering' error variety (often called 'Godless Dollars'), particularly on Washington and Adams coins. If the edge of the coin is smooth and lacks the date, mint mark, and mottos, the value can range from $15 to $50 even in circulated condition.

In 2007, the United States issued five different dollar coin designs: the Sacagawea 'Golden' Dollar and the first four entries of the Presidential $1 Coin Program (George Washington, John Adams, Thomas Jefferson, and James Madison). In circulated (Circ.) condition, these coins are common and typically trade at their face value of $1.00, though retail dealers may sell them for up to $1.50. A significant variety to check for is the 'Missing Edge Lettering' error, most common on Washington and Adams dollars, where the edge inscriptions (date, mint mark, and mottos) are absent; these 'Godless Dollars' can be worth $30 to $100 even in circulated condition. Other minor varieties include 'Double Edge Lettering' on John Adams coins, which can also command a premium.

The 2007 USA Dollar refers to either the Sacagawea 'Golden' Dollar or one of the first four issues of the Presidential $1 Coin series (George Washington, John Adams, Thomas Jefferson, and James Madison). In circulated (Circ.) condition, these coins are extremely common and typically trade at or near their face value of $1.00. Retail prices for individual circulated coins usually range from $1.00 to $2.00 to cover dealer overhead. A notable variety for 2007 is the 'Missing Edge Lettering' error (often called 'Godless Dollars'), where the edge inscriptions for the date, mint mark, and mottoes are absent; these can be worth $20 to $50 or more even in circulated condition. Standard varieties include 'Position A' and 'Position B' edge lettering, which refers to the orientation of the text relative to the portrait, though this does not typically add value for circulated specimens.

The 2008 US Dollar coins consist of the Presidential Dollar series (featuring James Monroe, John Quincy Adams, Andrew Jackson, and Martin Van Buren) and the Sacagawea Dollar. In circulated condition, these manganese-brass clad coins are extremely common and generally only worth their face value. While some collectors search for 'Missing Edge Lettering' errors on the Presidential series, standard circulated examples do not command a premium in the current market.

In 2008, the U.S. Mint produced five different dollar coins: the Sacagawea dollar (featuring the original eagle reverse) and four Presidential dollars (James Monroe, John Quincy Adams, Andrew Jackson, and Martin Van Buren). In circulated condition, these coins are very common and typically only worth their face value of $1.00. Presidential dollars from 2008 are notable for being the last in the series to feature 'In God We Trust' on the edge before the motto was moved to the obverse in 2009. While standard circulated examples carry no numismatic premium, collectors look for 'Missing Edge Lettering' errors (smooth edges), which can be worth $50 or more. Edge lettering also appears in two varieties: Position A (upside-down relative to the portrait) and Position B (right-side up), though these do not typically add value to circulated coins.

The 2008 US Dollar coins consist of the Presidential series (featuring James Monroe, John Quincy Adams, Andrew Jackson, and Martin Van Buren) and the Sacagawea design. In circulated condition, these manganese-brass clad coins are very common and generally hold only their face value. While collectors note variations in edge lettering orientation (Position A vs. Position B), these do not carry a premium for circulated examples. Retail value is typically face value, though some dealers may charge a small premium for convenience.

The 2009 US Dollar series includes the Native American 'Three Sisters' design and four Presidential issues: William Henry Harrison, John Tyler, James K. Polk, and Zachary Taylor. In circulated condition, these coins generally hold only their face value. Retail prices for individual specimens typically range from $1.00 to $2.00 depending on the seller. Varieties are distinguished by the mint mark (P or D) and the specific reverse design, with all 2009 issues featuring edge-incused inscriptions for the date, mint mark, and mottoes.

The 2009 US Dollar series includes the Native American 'Three Sisters' design and four Presidential issues (Harrison, Tyler, Polk, and Taylor). In circulated condition, these coins are extremely common and typically only worth their face value. No major high-value varieties exist for circulated 2009 strikes, though collectors occasionally look for 'Missing Edge Lettering' errors which are rare for this year.

The 2000 Sacagawea "Golden" Dollar is a common circulation coin with a face value of $1.00. In circulated condition, standard Philadelphia (P) and Denver (D) issues typically retail for $1.00 to $1.25. However, two rare varieties exist: the "Cheerios Dollar" (2000-P), which features enhanced, detailed tail feathers on the eagle, and the "Wounded Eagle" (2000-P), which has a raised die gouge across the eagle's belly. These varieties are worth significantly more, but the vast majority of 2000 dollars found in change are the common type.

The 2000 Sacagawea Dollar is a common modern coin with a total mintage exceeding 1.2 billion between the Philadelphia (P) and Denver (D) mints. In standard circulated condition, it carries no numismatic premium and is worth exactly its face value of $1.00. Collectors should check for rare varieties: the 'Cheerios' dollar (featuring enhanced, detailed tail feathers on the eagle), the 'Wounded Eagle' (a die gouge appearing as a raised line through the eagle's torso), and the extremely rare 'Mule' error (Washington Quarter obverse paired with the Sacagawea reverse). Unless one of these rare varieties is identified, the coin is considered a common circulation strike.

The 2001 Sacagawea 'Golden' Dollar was produced at both the Philadelphia (P) and Denver (D) mints. In circulated condition, these coins are very common and typically only worth their face value. There are no major recognized die varieties or errors for the 2001 issue that command a significant premium in circulated grades. Retail prices for individual circulated coins usually range from $1.00 to $2.00 depending on the vendor's markup.

The 1979 Susan B. Anthony Dollar is common in circulated condition and typically trades at its face value of $1.00. However, the 1979-P 'Wide Rim' (or 'Near Date') variety is highly sought after by collectors; it is distinguished by a thicker rim that nearly touches the date. In circulated grades (VF to AU), this variety can be worth between $5.00 and $30.00. Standard 'Narrow Rim' versions from the Philadelphia (P), Denver (D), and San Francisco (S) mints generally carry no extra premium unless they are in high-grade uncirculated condition.

The 1979 Susan B. Anthony dollar is a common modern issue typically valued at its face value of $1.00 in circulated condition. However, a specific variety known as the 1979-P 'Wide Rim' (or 'Near Date') carries a premium. On this variety, the date is positioned very close to the rim, which is thicker than the standard 'Narrow Rim' version. While standard circulated examples from Philadelphia (P), Denver (D), and San Francisco (S) are worth $1.00, a circulated Wide Rim variety can retail for $5.00 to $20.00 depending on the level of wear.

The 1980 Susan B. Anthony Dollar was produced at the Philadelphia (P), Denver (D), and San Francisco (S) mints. In circulated condition, these coins are extremely common and generally only worth their face value of $1.00. Unlike the 1979 issue, which has a notable 'Wide Rim' variety, the 1980 business strikes do not have major recognized varieties that command a premium. While they are no longer in active circulation, they are not considered rare by collectors unless in high-grade uncirculated condition or specific proof varieties.

The 1976 Bicentennial Kennedy Half Dollar is a dual-dated coin (1776-1976) featuring a special reverse design of Independence Hall by Seth G. Huntington. Because over 500 million were minted for general circulation between the Philadelphia and Denver mints, circulated examples are extremely common and typically only worth their face value. While 40% silver versions were produced at the San Francisco mint for collector sets, the standard copper-nickel clad coins found in pocket change carry no numismatic premium. Unlike the 1976 Eisenhower Dollar, there are no major recognized 'Type 1' or 'Type 2' lettering varieties for the Bicentennial Half Dollar that affect its value in circulated condition.

The 1999 USA Quarter series inaugurated the 50 State Quarters Program, featuring designs for Delaware, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Georgia, and Connecticut. In circulated condition, these coins are very common and generally only worth their face value. A slight premium may exist for the Delaware 'Spitting Horse' die crack variety, but standard circulated strikes from the Philadelphia and Denver mints do not carry significant numismatic value.

The 2007 US Dollar series includes the Sacagawea Dollar and the first four Presidential Dollars (Washington, Adams, Jefferson, and Madison). In standard Uncirculated (UNC) condition, these coins typically retail for $1.50 to $5.00. A highly sought-after variety from this year is the 'Missing Edge Lettering' error, particularly on Washington and Adams dollars, which can range from $20 to $150 depending on the grade. Satin finish versions from official mint sets also carry a small premium over standard business strikes.

The 2008 US Dollar coins include the Sacagawea design and the Presidential series honoring James Monroe, John Quincy Adams, Andrew Jackson, and Martin Van Buren. In Uncirculated (UNC) condition, these coins generally retail between $1.25 and $6.50 depending on the specific issue and mint mark (P or D). Notable varieties include 'Position A' and 'Position B' edge lettering, which refers to the orientation of the inscriptions on the coin's rim relative to the obverse portrait. While standard UNC examples are common, rare errors like 'Missing Edge Lettering' or high-grade certified specimens (MS-67 or higher) can command significantly higher prices.

The 2010 US Dollar series includes the Native American 'Great Law of Peace' design and four Presidential issues: Millard Fillmore, Franklin Pierce, James Buchanan, and Abraham Lincoln. In Uncirculated (UNC) condition, these coins are common and typically retail for a small premium over face value. While most specimens are standard, collectors occasionally seek out edge lettering errors, such as missing or doubled inscriptions, which can increase value. Prices vary slightly based on the specific mint mark (P or D) and the specific presidential subject.

The 2011 United States Dollar coins include four Presidential designs (Andrew Johnson, Rutherford B. Hayes, James A. Garfield, and Chester A. Arthur) and the Native American 'Wampanoag Treaty' design. In Uncirculated (UNC) condition, these base-metal 'golden dollars' are common, as millions were produced for each variety. While they are no longer found in general circulation, they typically retail for a small premium over face value. Specific varieties include 'Position A' or 'Position B' edge lettering, referring to the orientation of the inscription relative to the portrait, though this does not significantly affect the value of standard UNC specimens.
